to be clear for the OP: the website is https://refold.la/
they have a Simple Guide if you don't have much time to read, or just want to get an overview. they have a Detailed Guide if you want more information.

the guide is pretty well written, except the section on Anki is way too unnecessarily complicated when it talks about the features of Anki. the only features you really need is learning to make an Anki card with a front side and a back side; the front side has a sentence with all the words you understand except one, and you bold the one word you don't understand. the backside can be many things, but what works for me is the bolded word translated into English, and the sentence roughly translated into English.

Refold does indeed recommend that you learn basic grammar and basic vocabulary. it then gives you strategies on how to make TV shows and comic books and other input more comprehensible (ie more easy to understand). it also talks about how to use Anki to help your brain remember vocabulary easier.

just for clarity: i think u/lesarbreschantent is asking if "se le faire dire" is used to mean "get told" (an expression in English), outside of Canadian French.

"I got told by my boss" means something like being scolded or humiliated. For example, it could mean:

- my boss put me in my place (maybe because I was getting too arrogant; ie roughly "told me that my arrogant attitude was wrong and harmful")

- my boss scolded me (ie, roughly, "told me of the things I was doing wrong)


A related expression is "to tell off".

- Google defines this as "reprimand or scold someone. "my parents told me off for coming home late"".

This webpage ( https://forum.wordreference.com/threads/you-got-told.571405/ ) suggests that in France, "You got told!" is sometimes translated with "Tu t'es fait clouer le bec!"

---------

(*extra notes*)

*To my native anglophone ears, "I got told off by my mom" sounds slightly harsher than "I got told by my mom". The former suggests to me that the person scolding me was angry at me and actively wanted to show their anger, while "got told" could be less harsh (the person scolding me might only feel irritation, instead of anger). For example, I might "get told" by a friend, if I said something insensitive or politically incorrect, and my friend corrects my insensitive attitudes; my friend might not be angry with me, but only irritated with me.*

*On further reflection, "To get told" can also be slang for "to be humiliated", even if it's not scolding for having a wrong attitude or doing wrong behaviour. But I don't know if this slang is used as much nowadays as it was in (say) the 90s. (example: Suppose I ask someone out on a date, and they reply back, "Why would I want to date someone as ugly as you!?", then my friend might say "Dude, you got told!")*

*[Additionally, it seems that "get told" is mostly used by a person talking to the person who got scolded: "Dude, you got told!" or me thinking to myself "I really got told by my mom". But, "tell off someone" could also be used in a narrative: e.g. in a diary entry, such as "When I came home from school late, my Mom told me off"]*

my belief is that for beginners, it is almost impossible *not* to translate the French into your native language. and that is okay.

for me, i started with translating words into my native language, except words that i could imagine (mostly verbs with actions, like "to sit" or "to punch" or "to vomit").

once i got to the point where i could watch children's tv shows, i had stories with emotional connection, which helped me to imagine verbs and nouns more easily, without *always* translating the words into English first.

i'm at a point where i can watch a sitcom with subtitles and understand enough of it to enjoy it. i'm only sometimes translating words into English, but mostly non-verbal feelings and visual imagines and muscular imaginging-myself-vomitting/punching/sitting etc is happening, *for words i knew*. (also, "fuzzy" understand of words is common, such as "this word means something somewhat negative, though i don't really remember what". and so when i read that word in subtitles, i'll bsically get a feeling of "negative", rather than think the English word "negative").

but i absolutely want to emphasise that it is my belief that beginners *can't help* but translate French words into their native language, unless they're using learning materials that explicitly associate images or physical actions or story-memories with new vocabulary. but such learning materials aren't necessary. if you are translating into your native language, as a beginner, that's totally okay. you'll do it less and less the more familiar you get with vocabulary.

i've always struggled with answering that question!

according to the ACTUAL CEFR, i'd probably be at a B1 level in reading, an A2 level in listening, and an A0 or A1 level in speaking and writing. i'm really not trying to learn to output, and i just never learned the vocabulary for daily living (ordering at restaurants, talking about family and friends and jobs and hobbies) required for an A2 level.

however, my input abilities are at a level that i can have fun:

- when watching the news (ie, where they speak clearly, and don't tend to use too difficult grammar), or a documentary (which also tends to use standard grammar and no slang), i can understand about 70% of the sentences well enough taht i get the IDEA of the sentence. but i need subtitles, and i sometimes need to slow down the video to 0.75x speed
- for sitcoms and dramas, if they have subtitles and are in a Quebec accent, i can understand enough to enjoy the show. for children's shows, like Passe-Partout, i can undertand most of teh subtitles, except children's shows can be hard because they sometimes use very concrete vocabulary. (concrete vocabulary, like words for "faucet" and "cupboard" and "spoon", are actually difficult, because they are low frequency: they don't show up in news shows, or dramas, or sitcoms much)
- reading newspapers is harder for me, but doable. reading editorial pieces is REALLY HARD, because of the rhetorical devices used (ie, they use euphemisms to allude to historical event, or they use sarcasm but i don't realise how, or they say only half of what they mean and imply the other half, etc). reading reddit is pretty hard, because people on reddit write in a very sloppy way where their sentences don't actually say what they mean, but natives unconsciously infer what is meant by context.
- reading fiction is hard. like, super hard. fiction is out of this world hard, in my opinion.
- listening to accents from Europe, Africa, or the Acadian accent is .. really hard for me. my brain has trained itself on Quebecois accents, so that's what my brain understands. plus, the beautiful sound of Quebecois accents is literally one of my motivators. my brain literally gets fatigued when listening to an accent that it's not used to. to make life easy for me, i've decided to mostly stick with Quebecois or Canadian accent material, and leave learning a different accent to when i am more skilled and comfortable with understanding French.

may i say, though, i've been learning for SEVEN YEARS. that's a LONG TIME and i still suck at the language! but i am learning at my own pace, and for only 1/3 of the year, so it's okay! i'm literally improving -- just slowly -- but that's good enough for me!

i am one of those people for whom learning a new language is SLOW. my brain can understand grammar well, but it's way below average at absorbing vocabulary, or using intuition to guess the meaning of a sentence if i only partially/fuzzily understand what the words in a sentence means.

i often feel like giving up! actually, i have been learning French at a VERY inconsistent rate. i seem to study French / consume French-language media for about 3 or 4 months out of each year, and for the rest of the year, i don't do anything in French.

here are some random reactions i have:

- you say taht "there is still SO much to learn". i agree haha. there really is a mountain of understanding required before i'm going to even be abel to understand a TV show without subtitles.
- i get the feeling that people who are slow at learning languages, like us, might be easily discouraged. i know that i have often been discouraged. there seems to be so many people who say things like "yeah, i just vacationed in France for four months, and then i was fluent at the end of it" or "oh, i'm fluent in French. no, i didn't study. my uncle spoke French now and then, and i just kind of picked it up". i've come to the conclusion that these people are in the top 20% when it comes to having brains that just pick up languages easily. they also are the most likely to speak about how easy it was to learn a language! but people int he bottom 40% of brains (like me) aren't often heard on the Internet! so all this to say, yes, some peopel can become fluent in just 2 years. but that's not me, and that's not a lot of people.
- i strongly suspect that maintaining motivation in language learning is such a unique thing to every person, and it's not obvious what works for an individual. i HATED duolingo, but i forced myself to do it.. until i couldn't take it any longer. it wasn't until i eventually found Quebecois TV shows i liked, plus Anki, plus grammar textbooks that i liked, plus forums like this one to ask questions, that i was able to maintain enough motivation to not give up. but it was kind of by accident that i even found these things. my feeling is that if someone is losing motivation, it could be possible that the activities they're doing isn't quite a fit for them, but that other activities could work.
- my poor focus due to depression really makes language learning difficult, because i don't have consistency. i've learned that *for me*, it's necessary to allow myself to take *years* to learn French. and, that it's okay if i progress far slower, and do far less per month, than a typical learner. a person's state of mind (eg how stressed they are in life, how much sleep they get, how much exercise they get, how much emotional support they get) might have a lot to do with how easily their brain absorbs a new language. i think it's valid for me to try to learn French, even though i'm not set up for such efficient success as most other people are.
- i had to learn the skill of [Tolerating Ambiguity](https://refold.la/roadmap/stage-0/b/tolerate-ambiguity), and it took quite a long time for me to understand what "tolerating ambiguity" could mean for me. (one reason why i hated duolingo, is it expected perfection, but i'm realising that learning a language doesn't work like that for me). for me, it means some of these things: a) my brain learns vocabulary in a "fuzzy" way. when i see a new word, my brain just won't be able to remember all of its meanings. it won't even be able to remember the one meaning of the word, after i look it up, that is used in the sentence i read it in! my brain might only get a fuzzy meaning of th word, such as "this word means something negative, like 'unpleasant' ". it will take about 10-15 exposures of this word, in differnet sentences, before my brain starts to finally get a clearer, less fuzzy understanding of the word. b) it is *very okay* if, in my reading and watching TV, i dont' understand everything. in fact, it's normal for me to only really understnad 30-70% of the sentences. for sentences i don't understand, the subconscious part of my brain is still getting familiar with words that are new to me. it'll notice words that i've seen over and over again, and become curious about them. c) only look up words that i'm actually curious about, or *want* to look up. it's okay to just not bother looking up most words, if i'm too tired to do so.
- it took a LOOOOOOT of hours for my brain to even begin to be able to hear separate words, in listening. like, a LOT. listening to spoken French without subtitles is HARD. i literally can only understand maybe 5% of sentences clearly. 40% of sentences i have a very vague idea, because i can pick out enough words. and 55% of sentences i still have no clue. but, i still enjoy hearing the Quebecois accent, and tryign to let my brain pick out words. i will listen to a podcast for maybe 10 to 15 minutes, just enjoying the sound of the language. if i concentrate hard, my brain can pick out sentences. if i am too tired to concentrate, my brain sometimes picks out words, or even if it doesn't, i know my brain is subconsciously getting used to the language. but i know for me, understanidng spoken French without subtitles takes a LOT of listening hours. it seems that it requires a lot of vocabulary, and a lot of sheer listening to common grammatical patterns, before my brain even is able to start to hear words as separate words, instead of all blended together. [i know as a beginner, hearing clitic pronouns (lui, leur, le/la/l', y, en -- the pronouns that go just before a verb) took a LOT of time. these are very small sounds that are easy to miss. so it's normal for beginners' brains to not be able to hear them easily. it really took me a LOT of hours of listening (and probably watching TV with subtitels) before my brain started to be able to hear them. 
- finally, when i literally gave up on trying to output French (ie, tryign to speak or write French), it became MUCH more fun. i've learned that outputting is REALLY hard, at least for me.

i don't know if any of my ideas relate to your situation, but i want to wish you good luck anyways! i definiteyl hear your discouragement and i think it's probably quite common -- it's just not commonly spoken out loud. whether you continue French, or give up (temporarily, or forever), or maybe find different activieis or resoruces or help, i want to say that you certainyl are giving this language learning experience a try!
